title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: GAR — not norming God by human law; scandal reply
pass_a_gloss: GAR's second point: proposing the law against traitors does not mean measuring God's justice by human laws. Deniers say asserting first-sin imputation makes religion hated among Jews and Gentiles as cruel to God; the example shows what they themselves practice in public judgments cannot seem unjust to them. Not: men impute traitors' sins to children, therefore God imputes Adam's sin. Rather: Gentiles do not think it unjust if in lese-majesty a son suffers for the father—so who of them can charge God with injustice if he punishes Adam's sin in posterity? The example illustrates and vindicates; it does not prove.
pass_b_english: GAR. But as to what we add second: when we propose that law against traitors in this business, our mind is not that our thoughts of God's justice are to be measured by the norm of human laws. No such thought has yet entered our mind. But because those who deny the imputation of the first sin use this among other reasons—that our religion is brought into hatred with Jews and Gentiles by asserting this dogma, as attributing something unjust and cruel to the divinity—we teach by this example that what they themselves so often observe in their public judgments cannot seem unjust or barbarous to them. We do not therefore gather thus: Men impute fathers' sins to traitors' children. Therefore God also is to be thought to impute Adam's sin to posterity. But rather thus: To men, whether Gentiles or others, it does not seem unjust if in the crime of lese-majesty a son bears penalties for the father's sin. Who then among them can charge God with injustice if he punishes Adam's sin in posterity?—so that the example is used not to confirm the truth, but only to illustrate it and to vindicate it from the charge of injustice or monstrosity.
source_text: GAR. Sed quod secundo adjungimus, nobis legem illam adversus perduelles in hoc negotio proponentibus non ea mens est, ut putemus cogitationes nostras de Dei justitia ad legum humanarum normam exigendas esse. Nulla hactenus animum subiit cogitatio eiusmodi. Sed quia, qui peccati primi imputationem negant, hac inter alias ratione utuntur, quod religio nostra Judaeis & Ethnicis huius dogmatis assertione in odium adducatur, tanquam injustum aliquid crudele divinitati attribuens, nos hoc exemplo docemus, illis injustum aut barbarum videri non posse, quod ipsimet in suis publicis judiciis tam frequenter observant. Non ergo ita colligimus: Homines perduellium liberis peccata paterna imputant. Ergo & Deus censendus est peccatum Adae posteris imputare. Sed ita potius: Hominibus sive Ethnicis, sive aliis non videtur injustum, si in crimine laesae-Majestatis filius pro peccato patris poenas ferat. Quis igitur ex illis poterit Deum injustitiae arguere, si peccatum Adae puniat in posteris? Ut exemplum non ad confirmandam veritatem usurpetur, sed ad illustrandam tantum, & ab injustitia aut immanitatis accusatione vindicandam.
